title: Why can a bigger menu earn less?
principle: Every extra item you sell adds hidden costs.

screens.text: Let me take you to April 2020. India was in lockdown. Britannia, the biscuit maker, could run its factories, but with far fewer workers than usual. It sold many kinds of biscuit. Should it make all of them, a few of each, or make fewer kinds? Have a guess.

screens.prompt: With far fewer workers, what do you think Britannia chose to make?

options.label: Kept every product, a few of each, so shops stay full
Made only the products that sold the most
Made its newest products, to win new buyers

screens.why: It made only its best sellers. Britannia made about one in five of its brands, like Good Day and Marie, and those brought in about 80% of its money. Fewer kinds needed fewer hands. And every kind you drop is one less thing to buy, store and run.

screens.title: The cost you don't see
screens.text: Think of your fridge. Every new item needs its own stock, shelf and recipe, and it goes bad if it doesn't sell. That's complexity cost: costs that grow with every item but don't show on its price. A bigger menu feels like more sales. Often it's more cost.

screens.title: Now look at your bakery
screens.text: Now picture your home bakery. It's July, your fifth year. Your menu has grown to 18 items: six cake flavours, cupcakes, cookies, breads, the party pack and more. Your chocolate cake sells for ₹850; you keep ₹450. You're so busy you turn away about 3 chocolate orders a month.

screens.prompt: Pineapple cake: 3 sold a month, ₹450 kept on each. ₹1,000 of its fruit and cream goes bad each month. What does it really earn?
screens.why: Exactly. 3 cakes × ₹450 is ₹1,350. Take away the ₹1,000 of fruit and cream you throw away, and the pineapple cake really earns ₹350 a month. The waste was a hidden cost: it never showed on the cake's price.

wrong.a: I see what you did: 3 × ₹450 = ₹1,350. But that's before the waste. Take away the ₹1,000 of pineapple and cream you throw away, and it earns only ₹350 a month.
wrong.b: It doesn't lose money. 3 × ₹450 = ₹1,350, and ₹1,350 minus ₹1,000 of waste leaves ₹350 a month. It still earns a little.

screens.prompt: Pineapple earns ₹350 and takes 5 hours a month. In those hours you could bake 3 chocolate cakes you turn away. Which pays more?
screens.why: Right. 3 chocolate cakes × ₹450 is ₹1,350, almost four times the pineapple cake's ₹350. Your time is a hidden cost too. Every hour spent on a slow item is an hour taken from an item people already want.

wrong.a: Variety can bring people in. But here people are already asking for chocolate, and you turn them away. 3 × ₹450 = ₹1,350 beats the pineapple cake's ₹350.
wrong.c: Let's check. 3 chocolate cakes × ₹450 = ₹1,350. The pineapple cake earns ₹350. That's ₹1,000 more for the same 5 hours.

screens.prompt: It costs you ₹400 to make one cake. I'll show you six costs. For each one, tell me: is it inside that ₹400, or hidden?

items.text: Flour, sugar and cocoa in each cake
Cream thrown away because it went bad
The box each cake goes in
Hours spent learning a new recipe
The candle you give with each cake
Fridge space for 18 kinds of stock

screens.why: Exactly. Flour, the box and the candle go into every cake, so they're inside the ₹400. Waste, learning time and fridge space grow with every item you add, but no single cake's price shows them. That's why a long menu can quietly eat your profit.

screens.prompt: With 18 items, ₹15,000 of stock sits on your shelves. With only your 8 best sellers, you'd need ₹6,000. What does cutting give you?
screens.why: Exactly. ₹15,000 minus ₹6,000 is ₹9,000 that no longer sits on a shelf. Remember frozen cash from Unit 1: money in stock can't pay a bill. You get ₹9,000 back once. After that, less money sits on the shelf.

wrong.b: Not every month. You get it back once. ₹15,000 minus ₹6,000 is ₹9,000 of cash that no longer sits on a shelf, the frozen cash from Unit 1.
wrong.c: Stock is money you've already spent. ₹15,000 minus ₹6,000 means ₹9,000 you no longer have to keep tied up on a shelf. That's cash you can use.

screens.setup: It's July. Four customers ask for mango cake. About 6 would sell a month, leaving you ₹2,100 after the mango that goes bad, and it takes 5 hours a month. Pineapple earns ₹350 and coffee ₹150, and each takes 5 hours. Every 5 free hours means 3 more chocolate cakes: ₹1,350.
screens.question: What do you do about the mango cake?

options.label: Add mango, and keep every other cake
options.outcome: Mango earns ₹2,100. But its 5 hours have to come from somewhere, so you turn away 3 more chocolate cakes: ₹1,350 lost. All in, you gain ₹750 a month, and your menu grows to 19 items.
options.why: Mango was a good add. But every new item brings new hidden costs, here 5 hours of your time, so it should push out a weak item.
options.better: Add mango, and drop pineapple and coffee.

options.label: Add mango, and drop only pineapple
options.outcome: You lose pineapple's ₹350, and mango earns ₹2,100. Mango uses the 5 hours pineapple took, so no time is left for extra chocolate cakes. You gain ₹1,750 a month. Coffee still earns only ₹150 for 5 hours, and your menu stays at 18.
options.why: A good swap, but you kept one weak item. Coffee's 5 hours could have baked 3 chocolate cakes, ₹1,350, instead of ₹150.
options.better: Add mango, and drop pineapple and coffee.

options.label: Add mango, and drop pineapple and coffee
options.outcome: You lose the ₹500 that pineapple and coffee earned. Mango earns ₹2,100. You get 10 hours back; mango uses 5, and in the other 5 you bake 3 chocolate cakes you used to turn away: ₹1,350. You gain ₹2,950 a month, and your menu shrinks to 17.
options.why: Exactly. You let a new item in only by pushing out two weak ones. Your menu got shorter, your waste fell, and your hours went to cakes people want.

screens.text: Your menu grows from 10 items to 20. Sales may grow, but your ___ grows too: more waste, more stock and more ___.
screens.why: Exactly. That's complexity cost. Before you add an item, ask what it will really cost in waste, stock and hours, and what you could drop to make room.

summary: Complexity cost: every extra item (SKU) adds waste, stock and time that its price doesn't show.
Count what an item really earns: profit on each sale, minus the waste and the hours it takes.
Let a new item in only by pushing out a weak one.

cards.front: A cake earns you ₹900 a month, but ₹700 of its stock goes bad. What does it really earn?
cards.back: ₹900 minus ₹700 of waste is ₹200. Waste is a hidden cost.

cards.front: Customers ask for a new flavour. What's the smart way to add it?
options: Add it, and drop a slow item
cards.back: Every extra item adds hidden costs. Let a new one in by pushing a weak one out.

options: Each separate item you stock and sell
cards.back: SKU means stock keeping unit: each separate item you sell. More SKUs, more hidden cost.

sources.label: With limited workforce, Britannia working on 65% of its capacity (Agro & Food Processing, April 2020)
Britannia's focus on production of 20% brands amid lockdown brought in 80% revenue (DNA, 2021)
